narrative:
Your law school application was denied because the admission model estimated that you have a 57.6% chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. In other words, after weighing your academic record, the model saw failure as more likely than success, and that risk was the basis for the rejection.

The single most important factor in that decision was your Year 3 class standing. You finished in the second decile of your school cohort, while accepted students typically landed around the sixth decile. That gap was a strong warning sign: the model interpreted your later grades as indicating serious difficulty mastering the material, and it pushed the prediction firmly toward bar-exam failure.

Two factors pulled in your favor, but they were not strong enough to overcome that concern. Your LSAT score, though slightly below the average of 37.2 for accepted students, was still seen as a point in your favor—likely because it showed solid reasoning ability—so it shifted the prediction toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA did the same: at 3.50, it was above the accepted-student average of 3.23 and gave the model additional evidence that you can succeed academically.

In short, the decision came down to a contrast: your early academic record suggested capability, but your Year 3 performance raised a red flag. To strengthen a future application, focus on improving your final-year grades, retake the LSAT to raise your score, and consider additional preparation or a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous legal coursework.
